sections.title: Global Equities
sections.content:
October 2026 delivered a sharply bifurcated global equity tape, with the AI-driven technology sector's first major earnings reckoning triggering the Nasdaq Composite's worst monthly performance since March 2025, while energy-leveraged benchmarks and value-cyclical indices posted gains amid a relentless crude oil surge. The S&P 500 declined just **-0.9%** to close at **7,579.97** — a headline figure masking historic sectoral divergence — while the Dow Jones Industrial Average gained **+1.7%** to **51,771.14** and the Nasdaq Composite shed **-5.3%** to **25,437**: a spread of more than **700 basis points** representing the widest monthly Nasdaq-versus-Dow divergence of the current equity cycle.

Outside the US, the picture was broadly risk-off. Asia-Pacific indices retreated meaningfully, with the Shanghai Composite falling **-6.3%** to **3,599.02** and Japan's Nikkei 225 declining to approximately **63,290** — a monthly drop of approximately **-5%** (approx., verify before merging). European markets split along sector lines: the energy-heavy FTSE 100 closed at **10,729.78** and posted a monthly gain of approximately **+1%** (approx., verify before merging), while the technology- and industrial-oriented DAX underperformed, closing near **25,818** for an approximate monthly decline of **-3%** (approx., verify before merging). October 2026 reinforced the year's defining equity pattern: energy incumbents and AI sceptics diverge sharply whenever the AI spending narrative faces a credibility test.

sections.title: Your Must-Know Market Themes
sections.content: Four key themes that shaped markets this month:
themes:
AI Earnings Reckoning Triggers Worst Nasdaq Month Since March 2025 -- The singular catalyst of October 2026 was a cascade of catastrophic Big Tech earnings that forced the market to confront, for the first time, the sustainability of the AI capital expenditure supercycle. Alphabet disclosed quarterly AI infrastructure capital spending of **$51.4 billion** alongside negative free cash flow of **$9.1 billion** — a combination that sent its stock down **-12.6%** in a single session, the company's worst day on record and the second-largest single-day market cap destruction in stock market history. Intel compounded the shock, falling **-29%** on its worst day since the 1970s on weak forward guidance tied to a plant shutdown in Israel and ongoing PC market softness, while Amazon missed revenue expectations at **$201.9 billion** and reported a second consecutive quarter of negative free cash flow amid accelerated AI spending. Microsoft was the sole outlier, delivering Azure revenue growth of **+48%** with capex coming in below consensus — a narrow counterpoint that could not halt the broader de-rating.

The aggregate market impact was severe: over **$2 trillion** in Nasdaq-100 market capitalisation was erased during October, and the Nasdaq Composite's **-5.3%** monthly decline was its worst since March 2025. October's earnings season did not kill the AI investment thesis, but it materially extended the market's assumed payback timeline and injected meaningful multiple compression into AI-adjacent valuations, raising the hard question of how long institutional investors can sustain elevated technology multiples when the world's most profitable companies are burning cash on AI at a record pace.

Brent Surges 15% to $113/bbl as Energy Counters Tech Carnage -- Crude oil posted its fourth consecutive monthly gain in October 2026, with Brent advancing approximately **+15%** to close near **$113/bbl** and WTI reaching approximately **$103–$104/bbl** (approx., verify before merging) — sustained by the ongoing US-Iran conflict's persistent disruption of Persian Gulf supply chains and the failure of IEA emergency strategic reserve releases to suppress the geopolitical risk premium structurally. The Brent-WTI spread widened to approximately **$10/bbl** by month-end as US shale production growth remained insufficient to offset the strategic supply gap, and the IEA characterised the cumulative disruption as historically unprecedented. US energy equities (XLE) surged approximately **+13%** in October, acting as a powerful counterweight to technology's collapse and the primary driver of the Dow's outperformance relative to the Nasdaq.

The persistence of oil above **$100/bbl** for a fourth consecutive month is becoming the central macro constraint for the global economy heading into year-end: it sustains headline inflation above central bank targets, complicates potential easing cycles, pressures energy-importing current accounts in Asia and Europe, and creates a structurally bifurcated equity tape in which energy incumbents benefit precisely when the AI growth narrative faces its most significant credibility test — reinforcing a barbell market dynamic that is becoming increasingly difficult for broad benchmark investors to navigate.

Federal Reserve Hawkish Hold Sends Gold to One-Year Low -- The Federal Reserve held the federal funds target at **3.75%–4.00%** on October 28 in a 10-2 vote, with FOMC members Lisa Cook and Beth Hammack dissenting in favour of an immediate **25 basis point** rate increase — the most explicit hawkish signal the committee has delivered since restarting the tightening cycle in September. Chair Warsh described economic activity as "expanding at a strong pace" while cautioning that "inflation remains elevated," and subsequent communications left little doubt that a December hike represents the Fed's baseline scenario. JPMorgan Private Bank publicly projected further rate increases in December 2026 and Q1 2027, cementing a higher-for-longer framework that the market had previously begun to discount.

Gold bore the full weight of this hawkish repricing, falling approximately **-6.6%** during October to close near **$3,875/oz** — a one-year low — as oil-fuelled inflation expectations combined with the Fed's hawkish hold to reinforce a rate narrative that erodes the investment case for non-yielding bullion. Silver fell below **$50/oz** for the first time in eleven months. Significant GLD ETF outflows accelerated the metal's decline as institutional investors rotated out of inflation hedges in favour of direct rate-environment positioning, marking a sharp reversal from the safe-haven bid that had carried gold to multi-year highs earlier in 2026.

Flight to Quality Triggers Sharp Treasury Rally Despite Stagflation Signal -- October 2026 generated one of the most counterintuitive fixed income moves of the current cycle: the 10-year Treasury yield fell approximately **-35 basis points** from **5.29%** to **4.94%** — the largest single-month yield decline of 2026 — even as Brent crude surged **+15%** to **$113/bbl** and the Fed delivered a hawkish hold with two explicit dissents favouring a rate hike. The explanation is a market hierarchy: the shock of over **$2 trillion** in tech equity market cap destruction triggered a flight-to-quality bid for US government bonds powerful enough to overwhelm the concurrent stagflationary signal, demonstrating that risk-off safe-haven demand can dominate even when the macro backdrop argues for higher yields.

The 2-year yield closed near **4.57%** (approx., verify before merging), producing a **2s10s spread** of approximately **+37 basis points** — a modest flattening from September's **+41 basis points** as short-end yields declined fractionally less than the long end. October's bond rally provided the first meaningful positive fixed income month of 2026 for duration investors, but its durability is questioned by a combination of elevated oil prices and an explicitly hawkish Fed that has telegraphed further tightening. The December FOMC meeting will likely resolve the tension: if the Fed hikes as projected, long-end yields may reassert the higher-for-longer trajectory that October's risk-off bid temporarily suspended.

sections.title: US Equities
sections.content:
US equity markets delivered a deeply bifurcated October, with the S&P 500 declining **-0.9%** to close at **7,579.97** and the Nasdaq Composite shedding **-5.3%** to **25,437** — its worst monthly performance since March 2025 — while the Dow Jones Industrial Average gained **+1.7%** to close at **51,771.14**. The defining catalyst was unambiguous: earnings reports from Alphabet, Amazon, and Intel stoked serious market doubt about the AI investment thesis, with capital expenditure cycles running far ahead of monetisable returns and generating negative free cash flow at companies previously regarded as the most capital-efficient in the world. Alphabet's quarterly AI capex of **$51.4 billion** alongside **$9.1 billion** of negative FCF triggered a single-day **-12.6%** collapse; Intel fell **-29%** on its worst day since the 1970s; Amazon missed at **$201.9 billion** in revenue and disclosed a second consecutive quarter of negative free cash flow. Microsoft was the sole outlier, delivering Azure growth of **+48%** with capex below expectations — but it could not rescue broader sector sentiment.

Sector dispersion was October's defining structural feature. The energy sector (XLE) surged approximately **+13%** — powered by Brent crude's advance to **$113/bbl** — while technology and communication services posted double-digit losses. The S&P 500's modest headline decline of **-0.9%** concealed a tape in which over **$2 trillion** in Nasdaq-100 market capitalisation was erased and sector divergence reached its widest reading since early 2024. The Dow's **+1.7%** gain in a month when the Nasdaq lost **-5.3%** represents a spread of more than **700 basis points**, the widest Nasdaq-versus-Dow divergence of the current cycle and a dramatic reversal of the year's dominant index-level narrative.

October's US equity session raised a structural question that will define Q4 earnings season: if the world's most profitable technology companies are generating negative free cash flow after two consecutive quarters of record AI capex, how long can institutional investors sustain valuations that embed multi-year payback assumptions? The October data did not answer that question, but it made the silence around it considerably more uncomfortable — and the rotation into energy and defensive sectors that characterised the month may signal that at least some investors have begun positioning for a more extended multiple correction in AI-exposed growth names.

sections.title: European Equities
sections.content:
European equity markets delivered a broadly positive October, with the pan-European STOXX 600 recording its best monthly performance since June — powered primarily by the energy sector's outperformance on the back of Brent crude's **+15%** monthly advance. The FTSE 100 was the regional outperformer, closing October at **10,729.78** and posting a monthly gain of approximately **+1%** (approx., verify before merging), as BP, Shell, and the broader integrated oils complex acted as powerful index tailwinds — reinforcing the structural energy-beta advantage the UK benchmark has maintained throughout the US-Iran conflict cycle. European markets stumbled on October 30 as late-month Amazon and Intel earnings rippled across global sector sentiment, but the monthly tape remained positive.

Continental European indices were more constrained. The CAC 40 closed October at **7,969.42**, essentially flat for the month, as its diversified composition between luxury goods, financials, and energy partially offset technology-sector de-rating pressure. The DAX underperformed, closing near **25,818** for an approximate **-3%** monthly decline (approx., verify before merging) from its September close — its more pronounced exposure to technology hardware, automotive, and industrial cyclicals left it vulnerable to both the AI earnings shock and continued concerns about Chinese end-market demand softness. The divergence between FTSE outperformance and DAX weakness crystallised a broader European equity allocation debate between energy-beta plays and industrial-growth names.

The European macro outlook for November is complicated by several concurrent headwinds. Oil above **$100/bbl** is reigniting consumer energy cost inflation across the eurozone and the UK, the ECB's December meeting faces conflicting signals between resurgent energy prices and below-trend domestic demand, and German export sensitivity to a subdued Chinese growth environment continues to weigh on the continent's most important industrial economy. The FTSE's energy-driven outperformance may persist as long as crude remains elevated, but it is accompanied by a deteriorating fundamental backdrop for eurozone growth that limits the region's re-rating potential heading into year-end.

sections.title: APAC Equities
sections.content:
APAC equity markets bore disproportionate October losses, with weakness concentrated in technology-sensitive benchmarks aligned to the global AI de-rating narrative. Japan's Nikkei 225 closed October at approximately **63,290**, declining approximately **-5%** (approx., verify before merging) from its September close — the index's sharpest monthly pullback since early in the current year. The Nikkei's losses reflected both the global technology sector sell-off, which hit Japanese semiconductor and AI-adjacent names hard, and continued Bank of Japan balance sheet adjustment via accelerated ETF sales that weighed on domestic sentiment at the margin. Yen weakness against the dollar — USD/JPY edging to approximately **157.56** — provided a marginal offset for exporters but was insufficient to prevent meaningful index-level losses.

China's equity markets extended their weakness significantly. The Shanghai Composite fell **-6.3%** to close at **3,599.02** — the worst monthly decline for the mainland index since Q4 2025 — as domestic investors reassessed AI hardware valuations following the global tech earnings shock, and the PBOC's decision to hold the Loan Prime Rate steady disappointed market expectations for targeted economic stimulus. The Hang Seng Index declined approximately **-3.4%** (approx., verify before merging) to close near **23,294**, as Hong Kong-listed technology names faced the combined headwinds of global risk-off sentiment, elevated oil import costs, and persistent foreign capital outflows. Post-month, Chinese regulators announced market support measures, signalling official concern about equity market stability ahead of year-end.

The October APAC tape reinforces a structural vulnerability building throughout 2026: both Japan and China carry concentrated exposure to AI hardware and semiconductor supply chains that amplify any correction in the global technology sector. The stark contrast between the FTSE 100's energy-driven gain and the Nikkei's sharp decline illustrates how decisively the US-Iran-conflict-driven oil cycle has rewarded resource-leveraged economies while penalising energy-importing, technology-oriented ones — a divergence that will persist as long as crude remains structurally above **$100/bbl** and the AI earnings cycle faces headwinds.

sections.title: Foreign Exchange
sections.content:
The US Dollar Index (DXY) traded in a narrow range throughout October 2026, settling near **101.96** — a modest gain of approximately **+0.4%** (approx., verify before merging) from September's close near **101.5** — as competing macro forces kept the dollar anchored despite a volatile backdrop. The oil-driven inflation signal and the Fed's hawkish 10-2 hold with two explicit dissents favouring a rate hike argued for dollar strength; the sharp technology equity sell-off and flight-to-quality Treasury demand, however, created ambiguous risk sentiment that limited DXY upside and produced one of the most range-bound months for the greenback in the current cycle.

EUR/USD declined to approximately **1.118** from September's close of approximately **1.136** — a move of roughly **-1.6%** (approx., verify before merging) — as the ECB's more cautious policy stance left the euro without the yield support needed to appreciate against an incrementally hawkish Fed. GBP/USD advanced to approximately **1.339** from approximately **1.325** — a gain of roughly **+1.0%** (approx., verify before merging) — as stronger-than-expected UK economic data bolstered the Bank of England's restrictive policy case. USD/JPY edged to approximately **157.56** from **156.40** at end-September — a modest yen depreciation of approximately **-0.7%** (approx., verify before merging) in yen terms — as the Bank of Japan maintained its gradual normalisation pace without delivering any policy surprise in October.

The October FX tape highlights a nuanced dollar story: the greenback is no longer uniformly benefiting from every macro shock in the manner that characterised the 2022–2024 tightening cycles. The interplay of safe-haven flows, tech-driven risk-off, and oil-inflation expectations created a congested FX environment with limited directional conviction. With November US midterm elections approaching, political risk premium is likely to generate elevated volatility in emerging market currencies and may produce episodic dollar demand that underlying macro fundamentals alone would not justify.

sections.title: Commodities
sections.content:
Energy markets dominated October's commodity narrative with extraordinary force. Brent crude posted its fourth consecutive monthly gain, surging approximately **+15%** to close near **$113/bbl** — extending the oil price advance that began with the US-Iran conflict's onset in February 2026 and now reflecting a durable geopolitical risk premium that IEA emergency reserve releases have been unable to permanently suppress. WTI crude advanced to approximately **$103–$104/bbl** (approx., verify before merging), the Brent-WTI spread widening to approximately **$10/bbl** by month-end, while US energy equities (XLE) surged approximately **+13%** — providing the primary counterweight to technology's collapse and the single most important driver of October's extreme cross-sector divergence in equity markets.

Gold experienced a sharp and counterintuitive reversal. Despite a concurrent **-35 basis point** Treasury yield rally — which would conventionally support non-yielding bullion — gold fell approximately **-6.6%** to close near **$3,875/oz**, its lowest level in over a year. The decline reflected the Federal Reserve's hawkish 10-2 hold with two members explicitly dissenting in favour of immediate tightening, oil-driven inflation expectations reinforcing a higher-for-longer rate narrative, and significant GLD ETF outflows as institutional investors rotated out of inflation hedges. Silver fell below **$50/oz** for the first time in eleven months. Copper traded roughly flat at approximately **$6.47/lb** (approx., verify before merging), held steady by modest supply disruptions even as Chinese demand signals remained subdued and a marginally stronger dollar applied headwinds.

The October commodity complex delivered a clear analytical verdict: this is a geopolitically driven energy cycle, not a broad demand-driven commodity supercycle. The divergence between energy's dramatic outperformance and gold's sharp reversal — despite a Treasury rally that would historically support both — illustrates unusual rate and inflation dynamics in which commodity markets are not acting as simple macro hedges but are instead being shaped by discrete geopolitical supply variables that conventional models struggle to price. Copper's relative stability amid broader volatility further supports the conclusion that demand fundamentals, particularly in China, remain insufficient to generate a broad-based commodity rally beyond the energy sector.

sections.title: Fixed Income
sections.content:
October 2026 delivered a sharp and counterintuitive Treasury rally, with the 10-year yield falling approximately **-35 basis points** from **5.29%** at September's close to **4.94%** at October month-end — the largest single-month yield decline of 2026. The move was powered primarily by risk-off demand following the Big Tech earnings collapse: the flight-to-quality bid for US government bonds proved powerful enough to override the concurrent inflationary signal from Brent crude rising to **$113/bbl**, defying conventional stagflation logic that expects simultaneous losses in both equities and long-duration fixed income. The Federal Reserve held the federal funds target at **3.75%–4.00%** on October 28 in a 10-2 vote — with two FOMC members dissenting in favour of an immediate **25 basis point** hike — confirming that the tightening bias remains intact even as bond yields fell sharply in the same month.

The 2-year Treasury yield declined approximately **-31 basis points** to close near **4.57%** (approx., verify before merging), producing a **2s10s spread** of approximately **+37 basis points** — a modest flattening from September's **+41 basis points** as short-end yields fell fractionally less than the long end. The market now prices a December hike as the near-certain base case, and JPMorgan Private Bank publicly projected further rate increases extending into Q1 2027, cementing a higher-for-longer framework. For duration investors, October's **-35 basis point** rally represented the first meaningful positive fixed income month of 2026 — a substantial relief after September's devastating sell-off that sent the 10-year to **5.29%** — though its sustainability is widely questioned given elevated oil prices and an explicitly hawkish Fed.

The defining fixed income anomaly of October is the decoupling of Treasury safe-haven demand from the inflation-policy framework: the largest yield rally of the year came in the same month that oil crossed **$113/bbl** and the Fed telegraphed further tightening. This decoupling cannot persist indefinitely — either the AI-sector correction deepens enough to suppress the real economy and force a genuine Fed pivot, or oil-driven inflation reasserts itself and bond vigilantes recapture the narrative. The December FOMC decision, expected to deliver a **25 basis point** hike, will likely determine which force prevails in shaping the 2027 fixed income outlook.
